Before the report

Front matter

Statement of originality

This report describes a data platform that I designed, built, tested and documented myself between September and October 2026. Every pipeline, query, test, figure and number in it comes from runs in my own Snowflake account and my own Power BI file. Where I have drawn on published material, it is cited. The report may be freely copied and shared, provided the source is acknowledged.

How I used AI in this project

I want to be open about how I learned. I used Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, as a tutor. Whenever I reached a topic I did not understand, such as incremental models, slowly changing dimensions, task graphs or masking policies, I asked it to explain the concept from the beginning: what it is, why it exists, how it works and what can go wrong. Once I understood it, I built that part of the project myself, ran it, broke it on purpose and fixed it.

Claude also reviewed my SQL and design decisions, helped me debug errors, and helped me structure and edit this report. The decisions, the build and the results are mine. The way I learned is something I am proud of: I treated an AI the way I would treat a patient senior engineer, and I made sure I could explain every line before I moved on.

Acknowledgements

My biggest thanks go to my friend, whose experience of being stranded during the Heathrow disruption started this whole project. When he told me what he went through, he planted the question that every chapter of this report tries to answer. Without that conversation I would not have had the idea, or the reason, to begin.

I also want to thank everyone who encouraged me while I spent my evenings and days off learning data engineering from first principles. This project was built alongside my job, and that support mattered.

In one page

Abstract

AERORESILIENCE is a data platform, built on Snowflake, that traces airline disruption from end to end: from a missing spare part, to a grounded aircraft, to a chain of late flights, to passengers and bags that miss their connections. Airlines keep this information in separate systems — flight operations, baggage handling, maintenance, supplier portals and reservations — so the chain of cause and effect is rarely visible while there is still time to act on it.

To build and test the platform honestly, I wrote a deterministic Python simulator that generates one week of a realistic airline network (21–27 October 2026): 472 flights, 81,439 passenger journeys and 69,370 checked bags, across 10 airports and 4 airlines, with 20 aircraft, 55 spare parts and 6 suppliers. Its source feeds are deliberately messy. They contain duplicate messages, files that arrive a day late, a supplier that changes its file layout without warning, an airport whose baggage feed quietly collapses, and a time-zone trap in which local times arrive labelled as UTC.

The data flows through a medallion architecture — BRONZE (as received), SILVER (cleaned) and GOLD (modelled) — into a Kimball star schema of 9 dimensions and 8 fact tables. I built the platform in five versions. V1 implemented the pipeline in SQL with 65 exact-value tests. V2 rebuilt it in dbt as 42 models, one SCD Type 2 snapshot and 117 data tests, proved the rebuild identical to V1 with hash fingerprints, and made the largest model incremental. V2.5 added a Snowflake Tasks graph with a reconciliation quality gate and an audit log. V3 added a Stream-driven near-real-time alert feed. V4 added role-based access, masking of passenger personal data and volume-anomaly monitoring. V5 added a Snowflake ML forecast and a four-page Power BI operations control tower.

The final dbt build passes every check: PASS=160, WARN=0, ERROR=0. Because the simulator is seeded, every test has an exact expected value, so the platform does not just look plausible — it reproduces the ground truth: 83.8% on-time departures, 2 cancellations, 23.0 aircraft-on-ground hours and 6.6 mishandled bags per 1,000 passenger journeys. It also surfaces the chains behind those numbers. One technical fault on EK103 from Mumbai to Dubai caused a 569-minute delay that spread to 8 later flights over four days and left 145 passengers misconnected. A wheel failure at Manchester, an outstation with no spare in stock, grounded an aircraft for 12 hours while the part was flown in from Amsterdam.

The main lesson is that a pipeline that runs is not the same as a pipeline that is right. The failures that matter most are silent ones, and the engineering around the SQL — idempotency, reconciliation, quality gates, audit logs, access control and honest documentation — is what makes data trustworthy enough to act on.

Summary for employers

If you only have five minutes, this page is for you.

What I built

An end-to-end data platform that connects airline flight, baggage, maintenance, supply-chain and reservation data, so that a single disruption can be followed through to its impact on aircraft, flights, passengers and bags. It runs on Snowflake, is transformed and tested with dbt, is orchestrated with Snowflake Tasks, and is presented in Power BI.

Why it is credible

  • Every number is tested against a known truth. The data is generated by a seeded simulator, so tests check exact values, not ranges. The final build passes 160 of 160 checks.
  • The rebuild was proven, not assumed. When I migrated from SQL scripts to dbt, I compared all 18 cleaned tables and all 13 star-schema tables with hash fingerprints. Every one matched.
  • It handles real-world mess. Duplicates, late files, schema drift, a silent volume collapse and mislabelled time zones were designed in, detected and handled — and documented as incidents.
  • It behaves like production. Re-runs are idempotent, the largest model is incremental, a failed reconciliation stops the pipeline before bad data is published, every run is logged, and passenger personal data is masked by role.

What it shows about me

I do not yet have office experience in data engineering. So I built the evidence instead: one serious platform, built the way a professional team would build it, including the parts that went wrong. I learned each concept before I used it, and I can explain every design decision in this report — what I chose, what I rejected, and why.

The story behind the project

Preface — why I built AERORESILIENCE

I did not choose this project from a list of portfolio ideas. It started with a conversation.

A friend of mine was trying to travel to India when Heathrow was disrupted. He was stuck, and when he told me about it afterwards, what stayed with me was not the event that started the problem. It was everything that came after it. Aircraft and crews ended up in the wrong places. Connections collapsed. Bags were separated from their owners. And the passengers, the people most affected, were often the last to find out what was happening and what to do next.

The information that could have explained that ripple already existed. It was sitting in flight systems, baggage systems, maintenance records, supplier portals and booking systems. It simply was not connected, so nobody could see the whole chain early enough to act on it.

That gave me the question this project asks:

If something goes wrong anywhere in an airline's operation, can we detect it, understand its downstream impact, and help people act before it turns into chaos?

I could not prevent the event that disrupted my friend's journey. But I wanted to understand the engineering that decides whether a disruption stays contained or cascades — and I wanted to find out whether I could build it.

I also had a second reason, and I want to be honest about it. I hold an MSc in Computer Science, but I do not yet have office experience as a data engineer, and I know that is the first thing an employer looks for. I am ambitious about where I want to work and what I want to do, and I did not want to ask anyone to take my skills on trust. So I decided to build the evidence: one serious, end-to-end platform, built the way a professional data team would build it — layered, tested, monitored, governed and documented — including the parts that went wrong.

I made a deliberate choice to build one deep project rather than many small ones. Every concept in this report, from dimensional modelling to incremental processing, task orchestration, data masking and forecasting, was something I learned first and then applied to AERORESILIENCE. I simulated failures on purpose: lost files, duplicates, late data, a supplier that changed its file layout without warning, and an airport whose baggage feed quietly collapsed. Then I made the platform detect them and recover. When something broke for real — such as a masking policy that admin roles silently bypassed — I traced the cause, fixed it, and wrote it down.

AERORESILIENCE runs on simulated data, not on a real airline's systems, and Chapter 8 is honest about what that means. But the engineering is real, every number in this report comes from my own runs, and it reflects what I want to do professionally: take disconnected, messy data and turn it into something people can trust and act on.

All I am asking for is the chance to do this for a real team.

Chapter 1

1. Introduction

1.1 The problem

Airline disruption is rarely a single event. It is a chain. A missing spare part grounds an aircraft. The aircraft's next flights depart late. Passengers on those flights miss their connections at the hub, and their bags miss them too. Crews run out of legal duty time, which can cancel flights that had nothing wrong with them. By the time the consequences reach the passenger, the original cause may be hundreds of kilometres away and several hours old.

In this project's simulated week, almost half of all delay minutes — 48.8% — were reactionary: delay caused not by anything wrong with the flight itself, but by an earlier delay passed along through the aircraft's rotation. That is the single biggest cause of delay in the data, larger than technical faults, weather and air-traffic restrictions combined.

The information needed to see these chains already exists, but it is split across systems that were never designed to talk to each other. Each one speaks a different format, delivers on a different schedule and has its own quality problems:

Source system What it knows Typical format and problems
Flight operations Departures, arrivals, delays, aircraft used Hourly messages; re-sends; outages
Baggage handling Every scan of every bag One file per airport per day; duplicates; local times
Maintenance (MRO) Faults, deferrals, repairs Change records (CDC); several versions per fault
Supplier portal Purchase orders, shipments CSV; layout changes without notice
Inventory Stock of each part at each store Hourly snapshots
Reservations and departure control Bookings, segments, who boarded CSV with personal data
Weather Alerts by airport JSON array with epoch timestamps

Connecting them is a data engineering problem before it is an analytics problem. You cannot answer "what did this fault cost us in missed connections?" until the fault, the aircraft, the flights, the passengers and the bags all share a trustworthy common model.

1.2 Aim

To design, build and operate an end-to-end data platform that integrates airline flight, baggage, maintenance, supply-chain and reservation data, so that the downstream impact of a disruption can be measured, traced and acted on — and to prove that the platform's output is correct.

1.3 Objectives

  1. Generate realistic, deliberately imperfect source data with a known ground truth.
  2. Ingest it into a cloud warehouse without losing or duplicating data, and prove completeness.
  3. Clean, standardise and model it into a star schema that answers operational questions.
  4. Test every layer against exact expected values.
  5. Rebuild the transformations in dbt and prove the rebuild is identical to the original.
  6. Add production capabilities: incremental processing, history tracking, orchestration with a quality gate, near-real-time alerting, access control, data masking and anomaly monitoring.
  7. Forecast operational load and present the results in an operations dashboard.
  8. Document incidents, decisions and limitations the way a professional team would.

1.4 Research questions

  • A dbt project of 42 models and 1 snapshot, with 117 data tests — all passing (PASS=160, ERROR=0).
  • 65 exact-value tests in the original SQL version (40 for SILVER, 25 for GOLD), all passing.
  • A parallel-run reconciliation proving that the dbt rebuild matches the original on all 31 compared tables.
  • Six designed incidents detected and handled, one written up as a formal incident report.
  • Ten business questions answered, including disruption chains traced across aircraft, flights, passengers and bags.
  • A Snowflake Tasks graph, a near-real-time alert feed, role-based access, PII masking, volume monitoring and a forecast.

Chapter 2

2. Background and literature review

This chapter explains the two worlds the project sits between: how airline operations break down, and the data engineering ideas used to make that breakdown visible.

2.1 How airline disruption spreads

An airline schedule is a tightly coupled network. Each aircraft flies a rotation — a sequence of flights through the day — and each hub airport groups arriving and departing flights into banks so that passengers can connect between them. A delay to one flight therefore spreads along two paths at once:

  1. Along the aircraft's rotation. If the aircraft lands late, its next flight leaves late, and so on, until slack in the schedule absorbs the delay.
  2. Through the hub. Passengers and bags on a late inbound flight may miss their onward flights. A missed connection turns a short delay into a much longer one — often a rebooking onto a flight hours later.

Delay caused by an earlier delay is called reactionary or knock-on delay. European delay reporting has long shown it to be one of the largest causes of delay minutes (EUROCONTROL CODA). The same pattern appears clearly in this project's data: 48.8% of all delay minutes were reactionary.

Three operational areas sit behind most disruption chains, and each is run from a different system:

  • Maintenance and spare parts. When a fault is found, the aircraft's Minimum Equipment List (MEL) says whether it may still fly. A NO-GO item grounds the aircraft until it is repaired; a GO-IF item allows flight under conditions; a GO item can be deferred. If the part needed for a NO-GO repair is not stocked at that airport, it must be shipped in, and the aircraft is aircraft on ground (AOG) until it arrives.
  • Baggage. Transfer bags must move from one aircraft to another within the airport's minimum connection time. Mishandling is usually reported per 1,000 passengers (SITA Baggage IT Insights), and transfer bags are disproportionately affected.
  • Supply chain. Suppliers deliver parts against purchase orders. Late deliveries and poor visibility of stock across the network drive AOG time, and industry bodies have called for better supply-chain data visibility for exactly this reason (IATA).

The premise of this project is that integrating these areas is what makes the chain visible.

2.2 Warehouses, lakes and the lakehouse

A data warehouse stores structured, cleaned and integrated data that is optimised for analytical queries. Inmon (2005) described it as a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile collection of data that supports decisions. Kimball and Ross (2013) emphasised building it from business-process-centred star schemas.

A data lake takes the opposite approach: it stores raw data in any format at low cost, and applies structure only when the data is read (schema-on-read). Lakes are flexible, but without discipline they become hard to trust.

The lakehouse combines the two: open, low-cost storage with warehouse features such as transactions, schema management and governance (Armbrust et al., 2021).

Snowflake, used in this project, is a cloud data platform that separates storage from compute (Dageville et al., 2016). Data is stored once, and any number of independently sized virtual warehouses can query it. Warehouses start on demand, suspend when idle and can be resized in seconds, so you pay for compute only while you use it. Snowflake also stores semi-structured data such as JSON natively in a VARIANT column, which means one platform can hold raw JSON feeds and modelled tables side by side. For this project that mattered: flight messages and bag scans arrive as nested JSON, and I could land them unchanged and parse them later in SQL.

2.3 The medallion architecture

The medallion pattern organises a platform into layers of increasing quality (Databricks):

Layer Holds Rule Why
BRONZE Data exactly as received Never changed after load; full lineage back to the source file and row Recoverability: if a cleaning rule is wrong, everything downstream can be rebuilt without asking the source to resend
SILVER Cleaned, typed, de-duplicated data One trustworthy version of each record A single place where quality problems are fixed once
GOLD Business-ready models Shaped for the questions people ask Fast, consistent answers for analysts and dashboards

The key insight is separation of concerns. BRONZE answers "what did the source actually send?" SILVER answers "what is true?" GOLD answers "what does the business need to know?" Mixing these makes every bug harder to find. In AERORESILIENCE this separation paid off repeatedly: when I found the time-zone trap described in Chapter 6, I fixed one SILVER rule and rebuilt, and BRONZE still held the original values as evidence.

2.4 Dimensional modelling

Kimball's dimensional modelling organises analytical data into facts and dimensions arranged as a star schema (Kimball and Ross, 2013).

  • A fact records a measurement of a business event: a flight's delay minutes, a bag's scan, a part's stock level.
  • A dimension provides the context used to filter and group facts: which airport, which airline, which date, which part.

The most important design decision is the grain: exactly what one row of a fact table represents. If the grain is unclear, joins double-count and totals drift. Kimball identifies three fact table types, and all three appear in this project:

Fact type One row per Example in AERORESILIENCE
Transaction Business event fact_bag_scan: one scan of one bag
Periodic snapshot Entity per time period fact_inventory_snapshot: stock of one part at one store each hour
Accumulating snapshot Process instance, updated as it passes milestones fact_bag_journey: one bag from check-in to delivery

Dimensions change over time — an aircraft can move to another airline or be reconfigured with a different number of seats. A Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD) Type 2 keeps history by closing the old row and inserting a new one with validity dates, so that facts can be analysed against the attribute values that were true at the time. Type 1, by contrast, simply overwrites, and history is lost.

Surrogate keys are system-generated keys used to join facts to dimensions instead of business keys. They protect the model from changes in source identifiers and allow SCD Type 2, where one business key has several versions.

2.5 ETL, ELT and dbt

In traditional ETL (extract, transform, load), data is transformed on a separate server before it is loaded into the warehouse. Cloud warehouses made ELT practical: extract and load the raw data first, then transform it inside the warehouse using the warehouse's own compute (Reis and Housley, 2022). ELT keeps the raw data available, scales with the warehouse, and puts transformation logic into SQL, which more people can read and review.

dbt (data build tool) brings software engineering practice to the "T" of ELT (dbt Labs). Each transformation is a SELECT statement saved in a version-controlled file called a model. dbt:

  • works out the build order from ref() calls between models, producing a dependency graph (a DAG);
  • builds each model as a view, a table or an incremental table, according to its configuration;
  • runs tests declared in YAML (such as unique, not_null, relationships) or written as SQL;
  • implements SCD Type 2 automatically through snapshots;
  • generates documentation and lineage.

The result is that a transformation pipeline becomes a codebase that can be reviewed, tested, versioned and deployed like any other software.

2.6 Data quality and observability

Data quality is multi-dimensional. Wang and Strong (1996) showed that data consumers care about accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness and believability, not just correctness. Most pipelines check that a job ran. Fewer check that its output is right.

Common checks include row counts, uniqueness, non-null keys and referential integrity. They are necessary, but some of the most damaging failures pass all of them. Consider a source that sends only 2% of its usual records, but sends them correctly. Every row is valid, every key is unique, and the file contains exactly as many rows as its header says. Nothing is "wrong", yet the data is badly incomplete.

Data observability extends testing with continuous monitoring of freshness, volume, distribution and schema over time, so that unusual behaviour is flagged even when no rule is broken. Chapter 6 shows exactly this failure — and how a simple volume check catches it.

2.7 Orchestration and near-real-time processing

An orchestrator runs pipeline steps in dependency order, on a schedule, with retries, alerting and logging. Apache Airflow is the most widely used open-source orchestrator; cloud platforms also provide native schedulers such as Snowflake Tasks.

A central orchestration principle is the quality gate: a downstream step must not run if an upstream check fails. Without a gate, a pipeline will cheerfully transform and publish incomplete data, and the dashboard will show confident numbers that are wrong.

Processing can be batch (on a schedule) or streaming (event by event, continuously) (Kleppmann, 2017). Between them sits change data capture (CDC): tracking which rows are new or changed since the last read, and processing only those. In Snowflake, a Stream records changes to a table, and a Task can be set to run only when its stream has new data. Together they give event-driven processing without separate streaming infrastructure.

2.8 Governance and privacy

Passenger records contain personal data, which the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 require to be protected and processed only where needed. Two standard technical controls are:

  • Role-based access control (RBAC): permissions are granted to roles, such as "analyst", and users are granted roles. Access is managed by job function rather than person by person.
  • Dynamic data masking: a masking policy attached to a column returns the real value to authorised roles and a masked value to everyone else, at query time, without changing the stored data.

2.9 The gap this project addresses

Each technique above is well documented on its own, and cloud providers publish reference architectures for integrated airline operational data hubs (AWS). What is harder to find is a small, complete and inspectable implementation that combines them on airline data, proves its own correctness, and shows what happens when sources misbehave.

AERORESILIENCE is built to be that: an end-to-end platform whose every number can be checked against a known truth, and whose failures are documented as openly as its successes.

Chapter 3

3. Requirements and methodology

3.1 Requirements

I wrote the requirements before building anything, and attached a way to verify each one.

Type Requirement How it is verified
Functional Ingest seven source feeds in their native formats (JSON, gzip JSON Lines, CSV, CDC CSV, JSON arrays) Every file reconciled against the delivery log
Functional Produce one clean, typed, de-duplicated version of every entity SILVER tests with exact expected counts
Functional Model the business as a star schema linking aircraft, flights, passengers, bags, parts and suppliers GOLD tests: business numbers match the truth; no orphan keys
Functional Answer operational questions, including tracing a disruption to its downstream impact Ten analytics queries
Non-functional Re-running any step must not duplicate data (idempotency) Re-runs produce identical counts
Non-functional Late, duplicate and malformed data must not corrupt results Designed incidents A–E
Non-functional Personal data visible only to authorised roles Masking test per role
Non-functional The pipeline must stop, not publish, when its input is incomplete Quality gate in the task graph
Non-functional Low running cost on a trial account XSMALL warehouse, 60-second auto-suspend

3.2 Why simulated data

Real airline operational data is commercially sensitive and contains personal data, so it is not publicly available at the level this project needs: bag-level scans, tail-level maintenance records and part-level stock. Public flight-tracking data covers flights only.

Simulation also gives something real data cannot: a known ground truth. The simulator is deterministic — it uses a fixed random seed (42) — so every run produces identical data, and every corruption it introduces is recorded in a manifest. That changes what testing means. Instead of asking "does this look reasonable?", every test can ask "is this exactly right?". When a test says 959 passenger journeys were rebooked, that is not an estimate; it is the number the simulator created, and the pipeline must reproduce it exactly.

3.3 Simulator design

The simulator is four Python scripts that run inside Snowflake using Snowpark, writing files to an internal stage. Each file states its grain in a header comment.

Step 1 — Reference data

10 airports, 4 airlines, 20 aircraft with planned fleets, 52 directional routes, 16 minimum connection times, 6 fictional suppliers and 55 spare parts, each part fitting exactly one aircraft type. Routes are directional because jet-stream winds make eastbound and westbound flight times differ.

Step 2 — Operations

First a plan (aircraft rotations through the week), then what actually happened: delays by IATA delay code, propagation along rotations, weather capacity queues, tail swaps when an aircraft is unavailable, cancellations, MEL-driven faults, spare-part stock, AOG shipments, purchase orders and hourly inventory snapshots. All calculations are done in UTC; local times are added only for display. The simulated week deliberately includes the European clock change on 25 October 2026, a classic source of time bugs.

Step 3 — Passengers and bags

Bookings are made against the schedule, but travel follows the actuals. That single rule is what creates realistic misconnections: a passenger booked on a 45-minute connection discovers it is a 10-minute connection when the inbound flight lands late. Missed connections lead to rebookings and mishandled bags. Passenger records contain synthetic personal data, so that governance can be tested properly.

Step 4 — Raw feeds: the corruption layer

This step turns the clean truth into the messy files that real, separate systems would deliver:

Feed Landing path Format
Flight operations flight_ops/date=YYYY-MM-DD/ Hourly JSON Lines messages
Baggage baggage/date=YYYY-MM-DD/ One gzip JSON Lines file per airport per day
Maintenance maintenance/date=YYYY-MM-DD/ CSV change records (CDC-style)
Supply chain supply_chain/.../date=.../ Supplier portal CSVs, stock snapshots
Reservations reservations/date=YYYY-MM-DD/ Bookings and segments CSV, with synthetic personal data
Departure control departure_control/date=YYYY-MM-DD/ Who actually boarded which flight
Weather external/weather/date=YYYY-MM-DD/ JSON array with epoch timestamps
Delivery log _control/delivery_log.csv When each file "arrived" and how many records it declared

One design detail shapes the whole platform: raw systems do not share a flight ID. Like real airline systems, they identify a flight by its flight number, its origin and its local departure date. The platform has to build its own reliable flight identity from those three parts.

The designed incidents (Chapter 6) are introduced in this step and recorded in the corruption manifest.

3.4 Technology choices

Need Chosen Alternatives considered Why this choice
Warehouse Snowflake PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Databricks Separates storage and compute; native JSON; Streams, Tasks, masking and ML in one platform; free trial

The main trade-off is portability. Tasks, Streams and masking policies are Snowflake-specific, so moving to another platform would mean rewriting those parts. Chapter 10 describes how the design would move to Airflow and Kafka.

3.5 Phased delivery

I built the platform in versions. Each version had to run end to end and pass its tests before the next one began. This kept the project shippable at every stage and made each new layer of complexity easier to debug.

3.6 Validation strategy

Three kinds of evidence are used throughout the report:

  1. Reconciliation — the number of rows loaded from each file must equal the number of records that file's source declared in the delivery log. This proves nothing was lost or duplicated in ingestion.
  2. Ground-truth tests — business numbers (on-time percentage, rebooked passengers, AOG hours, mishandled bags) must equal the values in the truth files exactly. This proves the transformations are correct.
  3. Parallel run — when the pipeline was rebuilt in dbt, its output had to be identical to V1, table by table, proven with a hash fingerprint of every row. This proves the migration changed nothing.

Together they answer three different questions: did we get all the data, is it right, and did our changes break anything?

Chapter 4

4. Architecture and design

4.1 Platform architecture

Data moves in one direction through five stages. Simulated source systems drop files into a date-partitioned landing stage. BRONZE loads them unchanged. SILVER cleans them. GOLD models them as a star schema. Analytics, alerts, forecasts and the dashboard read from GOLD. Orchestration and governance wrap around the whole flow.

Layer Snowflake location Contents Key design decisions
Landing BRONZE.RAW_STAGE Files under raw/<feed>/date=YYYY-MM-DD/, plus _control/delivery_log.csv Date partitioning, so loads and checks can target a single day
BRONZE BRONZE schema, 21 tables Every record as received CSV columns loaded as STRING (schema-on-read); JSON kept as VARIANT; lineage columns _source_file, _source_row, file timestamp and load time; idempotent COPY INTO
SILVER SILVER schema, 21 tables (dbt: DBT_DEV_STAGING, DBT_DEV_INTERMEDIATE) One clean, typed version of each record De-duplication; conversion to true UTC; latest CDC version; derived flight_id
GOLD GOLD schema (dbt: DBT_DEV_MARTS) 9 dimensions, 8 facts MD5 surrogate keys; grain stated for every table; all three Kimball fact types
Serving ORCHESTRATION, REALTIME, GOVERNANCE, ML schemas Task graph and run log, alerts, policies and monitoring views, forecasts Kept separate from the tested pipeline, so demonstrations never disturb it

The platform is set up by one idempotent script, 00_setup.sql, which can be re-run at any time. It creates the warehouse, database, schemas, stage and file formats using IF NOT EXISTS. Two settings in it matter more than they look:

  • The warehouse AERO_WH is XSMALL, suspends after 60 seconds idle and resumes automatically. On a trial account, cost control is a design requirement, not an afterthought.
  • The account time zone is set to UTC. Snowflake's default is US Pacific time; leaving it would silently shift every timestamp calculation by seven or eight hours.

4.2 The star schema

Every fact table has a stated grain. Getting this right is what stops facts double-counting when they are joined to dimensions.

Fact table Grain — one row is… Kimball type
fact_flight One scheduled flight: plan vs actual, delay minutes by cause, load factor Transaction
fact_flight_delay One delay cause for one flight (a flight can have several) Transaction
fact_bag_scan One scan event of one bag, in true UTC Transaction
fact_maintenance_event One defect; NO-GO defects carry AOG minutes Transaction
fact_shipment One shipment of parts, latest status Transaction
fact_inventory_snapshot One part, at one store, in one hour Periodic snapshot
fact_bag_journey One bag: check-in, first load and delivery milestones Accumulating snapshot
fact_passenger_journey One booking: planned vs actual arrival, journey status Accumulating snapshot

The nine dimensions are date, airport, airline, aircraft, route, supplier, part, delay code and passenger. A few design details deserve explanation:

  • Surrogate keys are MD5 hashes of business keys. A sequence number would change every time a table is rebuilt, breaking every saved report. A hash of the business key is identical on every rebuild.
  • flight_id is a degenerate dimension. It lives on fact tables without a dimension table of its own, because everything descriptive about a flight is already in fact_flight.
  • Routes are one row per direction. London to Dubai and Dubai to London have different block times because of jet-stream winds.
  • dim_part carries MEL criticality (NO_GO, GO_IF, GO), so any supply-chain question can be filtered by how dangerous a shortage is.
  • dim_passenger holds synthetic personal data and is the target of the masking policy described in Chapter 5.

The star schema as modelled in Power BI shows the same structure: dimensions on the "one" side, facts on the "many" side.

4.3 The dbt project

The dbt project mirrors the medallion layers, so anyone who understands the architecture can find their way around the code.

dbt folder Materialisation Count Purpose
models/staging View 18 Light cleaning, one model per source; no storage cost
models/intermediate Table (one incremental) 7 Business logic: de-duplication, time-zone correction, flight identity
models/marts Table 17 The star schema read by Power BI and analysts; grants and column descriptions re-applied on every build
snapshots SCD Type 2 1 History of aircraft attributes
tests/business_rules Singular SQL tests 6 Rules that must always hold
tests/ground_truth Singular SQL tests 11 Exact values for this seeded dataset

Staging models are views because they do very little work and are read only by the intermediate layer; storing them would cost money for no benefit. Intermediate and mart models are tables because they hold real logic and are read repeatedly. The configuration lives in one place, dbt_project.yml, folder by folder.

The full dependency graph has 61 nodes — BRONZE sources, staging views, intermediate tables, marts and the snapshot — and every node built successfully.

Chapter 5

5. Implementation

Each version below was built, tested and committed before the next began. Code excerpts are shortened to the lines that matter; the full files are in the repository.

5.1 Ingestion into BRONZE

BRONZE stores every record exactly as received, plus where it came from. Each COPY INTO reads files from the stage and adds lineage metadata from the file itself:

COPY INTO BAG_SCANS_RAW FROM (
    SELECT $1,
           METADATA$FILENAME, METADATA$FILE_ROW_NUMBER,
           METADATA$FILE_LAST_MODIFIED, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
    FROM @RAW_STAGE/raw/baggage/)
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'JSON_FORMAT')
PATTERN = '.*bag_scans_.*[.]jsonl[.]gz';

$1 is the whole JSON record, stored in a VARIANT column. The METADATA$ columns record which file and which line each record came from. Three properties make this safe:

  • Idempotency. Snowflake keeps load metadata for each table — a record of which files it has already loaded — and skips them. Running the same COPY INTO twice adds zero rows the second time. That means a failed pipeline can simply be re-run, with no clean-up first.
  • Lineage. Every row carries its source file and row number. Any value in GOLD can be traced back to the exact line of the exact file it came from. When something looks wrong, that is the first question an engineer asks.
  • Completeness proof. After loading, the number of rows per file is compared with the record count that source declared in the delivery log. Any file that does not match is reported.

CSV columns are loaded as STRING rather than their final types. If a supplier sends "TBC" in a date column, a typed load would fail or silently drop the row; a string load keeps it, and SILVER decides what to do with it, visibly. This is schema-on-read: BRONZE never rejects data for being imperfect.

5.2 Cleaning into SILVER

SILVER turns raw records into one trustworthy version of each entity. The main problems and the techniques used for each:

Problem in the source Technique
Exact duplicates (the same scan sent 2–5 times) QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY scan_id …) = 1
Messages re-sent with new message IDs Semantic de-duplication: same flight, same event, same content = one record
Maintenance change records (CDC) Keep the latest version per fault_ref
Mixed time zones Values ending in Z are UTC; values without it are converted from the airport's local time
No shared flight ID Derive flight_id from flight number, origin and local date
Inconsistent codes UPPER(TRIM(...)) on every business key before de-duplication

The de-duplication pattern appears throughout SILVER. ROW_NUMBER() numbers the copies of each record, ordered so that the preferred copy comes first, and QUALIFY keeps only row 1:

dedup AS (   -- Incident D: each scan repeated 2-5 times -> keep one
    SELECT * FROM parsed
    QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY scan_id
                               ORDER BY _source_file, _source_row) = 1
)

The ordering clause matters. Ordering by source file and row makes the choice deterministic: the same copy wins every time, so a rebuild always produces identical output.

The time-zone rule is, in my view, the most important line in the project. Dubai's baggage system sends local clock time in a field named event_time_utc. Trusting the label would place 18,125 bags on aircraft after the aircraft had already departed. The rule trusts the format, not the label:

IFF(d.event_time_raw LIKE '%Z',
    TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(d.event_time_raw, 'YYYY-MM-DD"T"HH24:MI:SS"Z"'),
    CONVERT_TIMEZONE(a.timezone, 'UTC',
        TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(d.event_time_raw, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS'))
) AS event_time_utc,
NOT (d.event_time_raw LIKE '%Z') AS time_was_local

A genuine UTC timestamp in ISO 8601 ends in Z. A value without it is treated as the airport's local time and converted using that airport's time zone. The flag time_was_local keeps the correction visible rather than hiding it: 86,149 scan times were converted, and a ground-truth test checks that exact number. If the source ever fixes its labelling, the flag will show it immediately.

5.3 The GOLD star schema and analytics

GOLD builds the 9 dimensions and 8 facts described in Chapter 4. Surrogate keys are generated by a single macro, so every table uses the same method. Then 40_analytics.sql answers ten business questions, each written to demonstrate a SQL technique as well as answer a question:

# Business question Main technique
Q1 How did the network perform this week? Conditional aggregation (SUM(IFF(...))), scalar subqueries across facts
Q2 What causes our delays — primary causes or knock-on effects? Star-schema join to a dimension + RATIO_TO_REPORT window function
Q3 Which airports are our weakest points? RANK() window function over an aggregate
Q4 Day by day: when did the network struggle, and was weather to blame? Date dimension + LEFT JOIN to events on a time window
Q5 Which single delays spread the furthest? RECURSIVE CTE: graph traversal along actual_previous_flight_id
Q6 Flight delay → passengers → bags → connections Multi-CTE pipeline, anti-join (planned flight not boarded), pivoting
Q7 If this part doesn't arrive, what does it affect? QUALIFY to find the first affected flight + RECURSIVE CTE for the chain
Q8 Where are we exposed right now? NO-GO parts with zero stock QUALIFY with MAX() OVER () to pick the latest periodic snapshot
Q9 Did parts arrive when promised? NULL-aware fact analysis (undelivered shipments)
Q10 Which airlines lose the most bags per 1,000 passengers? Two aggregates at different grains joined on a shared key

Q5 and Q7 are the heart of the project. A recursive CTE starts from one delayed flight and repeatedly joins to the next flight flown by the same aircraft, for as long as the delay keeps being passed on — following the chain in SQL exactly as an operations controller would follow it on a whiteboard.

Results are presented in Chapter 6.

5.4 Migration to dbt

I rebuilt SILVER and GOLD as a dbt project: 18 staging views, 7 intermediate tables and 17 mart tables. Each model is a single SELECT in its own file; dbt works out the build order from the ref() calls between them and draws the lineage graph shown in Chapter 4.

A migration is only safe if the new pipeline produces exactly the same data as the old one. "It looks about right" is not good enough when the numbers feed operational decisions. I proved equality with a parallel-run reconciliation: for every table, compare the row count and a HASH_AGG fingerprint between V1 and dbt.

HASH_AGG computes one hash value over a whole set of rows. The order of the rows does not matter, but a single different value anywhere — one character in one row — produces a completely different fingerprint. Comparing two fingerprints is therefore a cheap way to prove two tables are identical without comparing them row by row.

SELECT IFF(v1_rows = dbt_rows AND v1_hash = dbt_hash,
           'MATCH', 'DIFFERENT') AS result,
       tbl, v1_rows, dbt_rows
FROM pairs
ORDER BY result, tbl;   -- any DIFFERENT row sorts to the top

Every compared table returned MATCH: all 18 SILVER-equivalent tables and all 13 GOLD tables. Only then did I treat dbt as the main pipeline.

The final build ran 160 nodes — 18 views, 23 tables, 1 incremental model, 1 snapshot and 117 data tests — in 32.5 seconds, with every one passing.

5.5 Incremental processing

int_bag_scans is the largest model: 503,206 raw scans that become 468,261 after de-duplication. Rebuilding it from scratch on every run wastes compute, and at airline scale it would not finish in time. So it is incremental: after the first run, each run processes only scans that arrived after the newest one already stored, then merges them in.

{{ config(
    materialized         = 'incremental',
    unique_key           = 'scan_id',
    incremental_strategy = 'merge',
    on_schema_change     = 'fail'
) }}

with scans as (
    select * from {{ ref('stg_bag_scans') }}
    {% if is_incremental() %}
    where _loaded_at > (select coalesce(max(t._loaded_at), '1900-01-01'::timestamp)
                        from {{ this }} t)
    {% endif %}
)

Every line of the configuration is a decision:

  • unique_key = 'scan_id' with merge. New scans are inserted; a scan that has been seen before updates its existing row. A re-sent scan can never create a duplicate.
  • on_schema_change = 'fail'. If a source adds or removes a column, the build stops and says so, rather than silently creating a table that no longer matches its tests.
  • The watermark is arrival time, not event time. This was the key design choice. Incident E delivers files one to two days late. A late file carries old event times but a new arrival time. If the filter used event_time_utc, late scans would fall below the watermark and be skipped forever, silently. Filtering on _loaded_at picks them up.

A second build with no new files processed zero rows, as expected. In the lineage graph, Snowflake labels this model as a backfill job, reflecting its incremental behaviour.

5.6 SCD Type 2 history

snap_aircraft is a dbt snapshot that keeps the history of aircraft attributes. On each run, dbt compares the current aircraft rows with the last version it stored. If nothing changed, nothing happens. If a tracked column changed, dbt closes the old row by setting dbt_valid_to to the current time, and inserts a new row whose dbt_valid_to is empty — meaning "current". History is never overwritten.

{% snapshot snap_aircraft %}
{{ config(
    target_schema = 'DBT_DEV_SNAPSHOTS',
    unique_key    = 'registration',
    strategy      = 'check',
    check_cols    = ['airline_code', 'icao_type', 'body_type', 'seats']
) }}
select registration, airline_code, icao_type, manufacturer,
       model, body_type, seats, year_built
from {{ ref('stg_aircraft') }}
{% endsnapshot %}

I used the check strategy because the source has no reliable updated_at column; dbt detects a change by comparing the listed columns directly. The business key is the aircraft's registration, which is what identifies "the same aircraft" across versions.

After testing, the snapshot held 20 current rows — one per aircraft — and 2 closed historical rows, from two aircraft whose attributes changed.

5.7 Orchestration with a quality gate

A pipeline that someone has to remember to run is not a pipeline. V2.5 schedules the whole flow as a Snowflake Tasks graph that runs daily at 06:00 London time:

  1. T1_LOAD_BRONZE calls a stored procedure containing every COPY INTO. Because loads are idempotent, a retry is always safe.
  2. T2_CHECK_BRONZE reconciles rows loaded per file against the delivery log. On any mismatch it writes the failure to the run log and raises an error.
  3. T3_DBT_BUILD runs dbt build on the deployed dbt project: every model, the snapshot and all tests.

Because a failed task stops all of its children, T2 is a quality gate: dbt never transforms an incomplete load. The heart of it is a few lines of Snowflake Scripting:

IF (files_mismatched > 0) THEN
    INSERT INTO AERORESILIENCE.ORCHESTRATION.PIPELINE_RUN_LOG (step, status, detail)
    VALUES ('T2_CHECK_BRONZE', 'FAILED',
            :files_mismatched || ' of ' || :files_checked ||
            ' files do not match the delivery log');
    RAISE reconciliation_failed;
END IF;

Other production details:

  • The schedule uses a cron expression with an explicit time zone (USING CRON 0 6 * * * Europe/London), so it stays at 06:00 local time across the clock change.
  • Retries: TASK_AUTO_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 1 retries the graph once on failure, which absorbs transient errors without hiding persistent ones.
  • Audit trail: every step writes to ORCHESTRATION.PIPELINE_RUN_LOG — what ran, when, and with what result — so the history of the pipeline can be queried like any other data.
  • Deployment: a task cannot run files from a personal workspace, so the dbt project is deployed as a Snowflake object, and must be redeployed after every change. I learned this the hard way and wrote it into the runbook.
  • Cost: after testing, the root task is suspended, so the schedule does not consume trial credits.

I had originally planned to use Apache Airflow, the industry-standard open-source orchestrator. A local Docker and WSL installation problem on my laptop made that impractical in the time available. Rather than stall, I implemented the same orchestration concepts — dependencies, scheduling, retries, a quality gate and logging — with Snowflake Tasks, and listed Airflow as future work.

5.8 Near-real-time alerts

Batch processing once a day is too slow for an operations control room. A bag that has missed its connection needs action within minutes, not tomorrow morning. V3 adds an event-driven path:

  • LIVE_BAG_EVENTS is a table that receives bag events one at a time, as they happen.
  • An append-only Stream on that table acts as a bookmark: it shows exactly which rows are new since they were last consumed.
  • A Task checks every minute, but only runs WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA(...). An empty minute costs nothing, because the warehouse never starts.
  • When it runs, it inserts every event that needs action — MISSED_CONNECTION and HELD_AWAITING_REBOOKING — into REALTIME.OPS_ALERTS.
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK AERORESILIENCE.REALTIME.T_BAG_ALERTS
    WAREHOUSE = AERO_WH
    SCHEDULE  = '1 MINUTE'
    WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('AERORESILIENCE.REALTIME.LIVE_BAG_EVENTS_STREAM')
AS
INSERT INTO AERORESILIENCE.REALTIME.OPS_ALERTS
       (alert_type, airport_code, flight_id, bag_tag, detail)
SELECT raw:event_type::STRING, raw:location.airport::STRING,
       raw:flight.flight_id::STRING, raw:bag.tag::STRING,
       'Action needed: bag ' || raw:bag.tag::STRING || ' ' || raw:event_type::STRING
FROM AERORESILIENCE.REALTIME.LIVE_BAG_EVENTS_STREAM
WHERE raw:event_type::STRING IN ('MISSED_CONNECTION', 'HELD_AWAITING_REBOOKING');

Reading a stream inside a DML statement such as INSERT advances its offset, so every event is processed exactly once: it can neither be missed nor alerted twice. In the demonstration, three live events arrived — one normal LOADED scan and two that needed action — and exactly two alerts were raised, after which the stream reported no new data.

This feed lives in its own REALTIME schema on purpose. Demonstration events never touch BRONZE, so they cannot disturb the tested batch pipeline or its ground-truth numbers.

5.9 Governance

V4 answers the question every organisation handling personal data must answer: who can see what, and how do we know?

Role-based access. An AERO_ANALYST role can use the warehouse and read only the 17 mart tables — the star schema — and nothing in BRONZE or SILVER. There is a subtlety here: dbt drops and re-creates mart tables on every build, which would remove any grant made by hand. So the grant is declared in dbt_project.yml with +grants, and dbt re-applies it every time it builds.

PII masking. A masking policy returns ***MASKED*** for passenger name and email to every role except ACCOUNTADMIN. A dbt post-hook on dim_passenger re-attaches the policy after every build, for the same reason as the grant.

CREATE MASKING POLICY IF NOT EXISTS AERORESILIENCE.GOVERNANCE.PII_MASK
    AS (val STRING) RETURNS STRING -> '***MASKED***';

ALTER MASKING POLICY AERORESILIENCE.GOVERNANCE.PII_MASK SET BODY ->
    CASE WHEN CURRENT_ROLE() = 'ACCOUNTADMIN' THEN val
         ELSE '***MASKED***'
    END;

A real problem I hit. My first version of the policy used IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('ACCOUNTADMIN'). When I switched to the analyst role to test it, I could still see real names and emails. The policy looked broken. After investigating, I found the cause: Snowflake Workspaces keep secondary roles active in the background, so my admin role was still "in session" even after I switched to the analyst role. The policy was doing exactly what I had told it to do. I changed it to CURRENT_ROLE(), which checks only the active primary role, and the test then showed masked values as expected. I documented the remaining limitation honestly: role switching inside one user cannot fully prove least privilege, so a true access test needs a separate least-privilege test user.

I also learned a smaller lesson: a masking policy that is attached to columns cannot be replaced with CREATE OR REPLACE. The script therefore creates it with IF NOT EXISTS and changes its body with ALTER, which makes the script safe to re-run.

Volume monitoring. GOVERNANCE.V_BAG_FEED_VOLUME compares each airport's daily scan count with that airport's own median, and flags any airport-day below 30% of normal as a VOLUME ANOMALY. Chapter 6 explains why this catches a failure that every other check misses.

SELECT airport_code, file_date, scans,
       MEDIAN(scans) OVER (PARTITION BY airport_code) AS typical_scans,
       ROUND(scans / NULLIF(typical_scans, 0), 2)     AS ratio_to_typical,
       IFF(ratio_to_typical < 0.30, 'VOLUME ANOMALY', 'ok') AS volume_status
FROM daily
WHERE file_date BETWEEN '2026-10-21' AND '2026-10-27';

The window is limited to the operating week because the first and last days of the files are partial by design, and would otherwise be flagged as false alarms.

5.10 Forecasting and the dashboard

Using Snowflake ML's FORECAST function, I trained one model per hub — London Heathrow, Dubai, Doha and Amsterdam — on hourly bag-scan counts, and predicted the next 24 hours with an upper and lower bound.

CREATE OR REPLACE SNOWFLAKE.ML.FORECAST AERORESILIENCE.ML.HUB_SCAN_FORECAST(
    INPUT_DATA        => TABLE(AERORESILIENCE.ML.V_HOURLY_HUB_SCANS),
    SERIES_COLNAME    => 'airport',
    TIMESTAMP_COLNAME => 'ts',
    TARGET_COLNAME    => 'scans'
);
CALL AERORESILIENCE.ML.HUB_SCAN_FORECAST!FORECAST(FORECASTING_PERIODS => 24);

One statement trains a separate model for each value of the series column, so four airports cost no more code than one. A baggage operation could use such a forecast to staff handling teams for the next day's peaks. I am clear about the limit, though: with only one week of synthetic history, the model cannot learn weekly or seasonal patterns, so this demonstrates the method rather than a production-grade forecast.

Finally, the GOLD star schema was exported to Power BI, where I built a four-page operations control tower. Chapter 7 walks through it.

Chapter 6

6. Testing, incidents and results

Every test in the platform has an exact expected value, and every one passes: 40 SILVER and 25 GOLD checks in V1, and 117 data tests in the final dbt build, which ran 160 nodes with PASS=160 and ERROR=0.

6.1 Testing approach

Test layer What it checks Count Result
BRONZE reconciliation Rows loaded per file equal rows declared in the delivery log Every file All match
SILVER (V1) Row counts after de-duplication, unique business keys, parseable times, no impossible bag loads, delay codes sum to delay minutes, every booking resolves to a flight 40 All PASS
GOLD (V1) Business numbers equal the truth; no orphan keys between facts and dimensions 25 All PASS
dbt generic tests unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships, declared in YAML Part of 117 All PASS
dbt business rules 6 rules that must always hold 6 All PASS
dbt ground truth 11 exact values for this seeded dataset 11 All PASS
Parallel run dbt output identical to V1 by row count and HASH_AGG 18 + 13 tables All MATCH

The two kinds of singular dbt test are deliberately tagged differently, because a failure means different things:

  • A business-rule test encodes something that must be true of any airline data: an aircraft cannot be in two places at once; a bag cannot be loaded after its flight has left; a flight cannot board more passengers than it has seats; delay causes must add up to the total delay. A failure here always means a bug in the pipeline.
  • A ground-truth test encodes a value that is true of this seeded dataset only: 1,223 flight events after de-duplication, 959 rebooked journeys, 23 AOG hours. A failure here means something changed — the code or the data — and needs investigating.

The V1 tests use a simple and readable pattern. Each check states its expected value and its actual value, and the query prints PASS or FAIL, with failures sorted to the top:

WITH checks AS (
              SELECT 'airports: rows' AS check_name, '10' AS expected,
                     (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AIRPORTS)::STRING AS actual
    UNION ALL SELECT 'airlines: rows', '4', (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AIRLINES)::STRING
    -- ... 38 more checks
)
SELECT IFF(expected = actual, 'PASS', 'FAIL') AS result, check_name, expected, actual
FROM checks
ORDER BY result, check_name;      -- any FAIL appears at the top

The row counts across all layers give a sense of scale. Bag scans dominate: 503,206 raw scans in BRONZE become 468,261 in SILVER after de-duplication.

6.2 Designed incidents

Each incident was injected by the simulator, recorded in the corruption manifest, and then detected and handled by the platform.

Incident What the source did How the platform handled it Evidence
A — Outage and backfill One hour of flight messages lost, then re-sent the next morning A full rebuild from BRONZE absorbs the late file 1,253 raw messages → 1,223 unique flight events, matching the truth
B — Schema drift On 25 October the supplier renamed part_number to component_id and added carrier_name Detected by header inspection; fixed with name-based loading and schema evolution; daily drift check added Formal incident report
C — Silent volume collapse Frankfurt's baggage feed sent about 2% of its normal scans for one day Reconciliation passed (the file was honest about its size). The volume view flagged FRA on 24 October; GOLD labels 317 bags UNKNOWN_NO_FINAL_SCAN rather than guessing Ground-truth test: 317
D — Duplicates Scans repeated 2–5 times; messages re-sent with new IDs Key de-duplication plus semantic de-duplication 503,206 raw scans → 468,261
E — Late data Events delivered 1–2 days late Full rebuilds include them; the incremental watermark on arrival time picks them up; a received_late flag marks them Ground-truth counts match
Time-zone trap Dubai sent local time in a field named event_time_utc No Z suffix → treated as local time and converted 86,149 times converted; without the fix, 18,125 bags would appear loaded after departure

Incident B in detail: schema drift

Incident B is written up as a formal incident report in the repository, following the structure a real team would use: detect, assess impact, fix, prevent, write up.

  • Detect. Before designing the supplier load, I inspected the first line — the header — of every supplier file. Grouping identical headers showed two different layouts, with the change starting on 25 October.
  • Impact. The standard load reads CSV columns by position. With the new layout it would have silently dropped carrier_name and relied on luck for component_id landing in the right column. No error would have been raised.
  • Fix. I switched the supplier feeds to name-based loading (MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME) with schema evolution enabled, so every value lands in the correctly named column and new columns are added automatically. Old rows keep part_number; new rows have component_id. Nothing was lost.
  • Prevent. A daily drift check compares each file's header with the previous file from the same feed and flags any change as SCHEMA DRIFT, using a LAG() window function.

Two problems the tests found

Two further problems were not designed in. The tests found them, which is exactly what tests are for:

  • Business-key collision. The same flight number could appear twice from the same origin on the same local day, which made flight_id ambiguous. A uniqueness test failed. I traced it to the generator, fixed it, and kept the test, which now shows zero ambiguous keys.
  • Masking bypass. Described in Section 5.9: secondary roles made the masking test pass for the wrong reason until I changed the policy to use CURRENT_ROLE().

The most important lesson: Incident C

Incident C taught me the difference between testing and observability. Every standard check passed. The Frankfurt file contained exactly the number of rows its header declared. Every scan was valid, every key unique, every timestamp parseable. By the rules, the data was perfect — and yet 98% of a day's scans at Frankfurt were missing.

Only comparing the volume with Frankfurt's own normal level revealed the problem. The volume view flagged it, and the analytics traced the impact to British Airways and KLM, the airlines serving Frankfurt in the simulation. GOLD did the honest thing with the affected bags: instead of guessing that they were delivered, it labelled 317 bags UNKNOWN_NO_FINAL_SCAN. A dashboard that hides uncertainty is worse than one that admits it.

6.3 Results: the simulated week (21–27 October 2026)

Measure Result
Flights scheduled / cancelled 472 / 2
On-time departures (less than 15 minutes late) 83.8%
Share of delay minutes that were reactionary (knock-on) 48.8% — the largest single cause
Passenger journeys / arriving 15 or more minutes late 81,439 / 27.3%
Journeys completed as planned / rebooked 98.7% / 1.18% (959 journeys)
Average load factor 84.8%
Checked bags 69,370
Mishandled bags 6.6 per 1,000 passenger journeys (7.7 per 1,000 bags)
Aircraft-on-ground hours from NO-GO faults 23.0

A note on the mishandled-bag figure, because it appears as two numbers in my work. The SQL headline (Q1) divides mishandled bags by passenger journeys and gives 6.6 per 1,000. The Power BI card divides the same mishandled bags by checked bags and gives 7.73 per 1,000. Both are correct; they use different denominators. Industry reports usually quote mishandling per 1,000 passengers, so 6.6 is the headline figure in this report. Being precise about definitions like this matters: two teams quoting "the mishandling rate" with different denominators is how meetings go wrong.

Three findings stand out:

  1. Knock-on delay is the biggest problem. 48.8% of delay minutes came from aircraft arriving late from a previous flight — more than technical faults, weather, air-traffic restrictions and ramp handling combined.
  2. Passengers suffer more than flights. Only 16.2% of flights departed late, but 27.3% of passenger journeys arrived late. A short flight delay can become a missed connection, and a missed connection can become an arrival hours later. Measuring punctuality by flight understates what passengers experience.
  3. Mishandling concentrates at the hub carriers. Emirates mishandled 20.3 bags per 1,000 passengers against British Airways' 1.2. The pattern points to hub-transfer exposure: the more bags that have to make a connection at a hub, the more chances there are for one to miss it.

6.4 Tracing disruption chains

The project's central question — if this part doesn't arrive, what does it affect? — is answered by queries Q5 to Q7.

  1. Technical faultEK103 Mumbai → Dubai
  2. 569 mindeparture delay
  3. 8 flightsdelayed over 4 days
  4. 145passengers misconnected
  5. 46bags mishandled

EK103, Mumbai to Dubai. A technical fault delayed departure by 569 minutes. Through the aircraft's rotation, the delay was passed on to 8 later flights over four days. At the Dubai hub, 145 passengers misconnected and 46 bags were mishandled. Following this chain needs the flight system (the delay), the aircraft rotation (who flew next), the booking system (who was connecting) and the baggage system (which bags followed them) — four systems, one story.

FLT-0010, PH-JLV at Manchester. A main-wheel failure — a NO-GO item under the MEL — grounded the aircraft at Manchester, an outstation with no spare wheel in stock. The part was transferred from KLM's store in Amsterdam. The aircraft spent 12 hours (720 minutes) on the ground, and its next flight left 669 minutes late. The Power BI supply-chain page shows this event and one more: a second NO-GO grounding of 660 minutes, resolved with a part transferred from Dubai. Together they account for all 1,380 AOG minutes — exactly the 23.0 hours in the headline.

Neither chain is visible in any single source system. The flight system sees a late departure. The maintenance system sees a defect. The baggage system sees misrouted bags. Only the integrated model connects them into one story with a cause — and that is the whole argument for the platform.

Chapter 7

7. The operations control tower

The Power BI report turns the star schema into four pages, each answering one question an operations manager would ask. The model is imported from the GOLD exports and uses the same star schema as Snowflake.

7.1 The data model

Each relationship runs from a fact (the "many" side) to a dimension (the "one" side), with filters flowing from dimensions to facts. That is the star schema working as designed.

One relationship is deliberately inactive: FACT_FLIGHT_DELAY to FACT_FLIGHT on FLIGHT_ID. Both facts already relate to the same dimensions (date, airline, airport). An active link between them would create two filter paths between the same tables, which Power BI cannot resolve unambiguously. Keeping it inactive avoids that ambiguity; it can still be switched on inside a specific measure with USERELATIONSHIP when needed.

7.2 Page 1 — Overview: how did the network perform?

The headline cards match the SQL ground truth exactly: 472 flights, 23 AOG hours, 83.8% on time and 2 cancellations. The daily trend shows the network struggling on 22 October, when on-time performance fell to about 69%, before recovering to about 94% by 26 October. The final point, 28 October, drops to about 50% because that day is only partly inside the simulated week; only a handful of flights fall on it. I keep it visible but explain it, rather than hiding it — the same principle as the edge-day filter in the volume monitor.

By airline, Qatar Airways leads at about 96% on time, with KLM, Emirates and British Airways each between about 80% and 82%.

7.3 Page 2 — Delay: where does delay come from?

The page leads with its finding in words: half of delay is a knock-on from earlier flights. The cause chart makes it obvious — reactionary delay (about 3,000 minutes) is more than twice the next cause, aircraft technical defects (about 1,200 minutes), followed by weather, air-traffic flow restrictions and ramp handling.

By airport, Manchester has the highest average departure delay at about 37 minutes, followed by New York JFK and Mumbai. Doha has almost none. Manchester's position fits the supply-chain story: it is an outstation where an aircraft was grounded waiting for a part.

7.4 Page 3 — Passengers and bags: who felt the impact?

Almost every bag was delivered with its passenger, but the small categories are the ones that matter operationally: mishandled and delivered late, unknown with no final scan (the 317 Frankfurt bags from Incident C), and bags still in transit when the week ended. By airline, Emirates mishandles far more bags than anyone else, followed by Qatar Airways — the two hub carriers — with KLM and British Airways far lower. Of 81,000 journeys, 98.7% went as planned and 1.18% were rebooked.

7.5 Page 4 — Supply chain: stock-outs and aircraft on ground

This page connects parts to operations. There were about 3,900 part-hours of stock-outs across the week — about 2,700 for GO-IF parts and about 1,200 for NO-GO parts. The table on the left shows the only two events that actually grounded aircraft: 720 minutes waiting for a part transferred from Amsterdam and 660 minutes for a part transferred from Dubai. Every other defect was fixed from local stock, or was a GO or GO-IF item that let the aircraft keep flying.

The right-hand table is the actionable part: it lists each part and airport that ran out, and for how long. Many NO-GO parts were out of stock for the whole week (168 hours) at hubs such as Heathrow, Doha and Dubai. Most of the time that did not matter, because no aircraft needed those parts. But it is exactly the exposure a supply-chain manager would want to see before the next fault, not after it — and it is what query Q8 reports in SQL.

Chapter 8

8. Evaluation and limitations

The platform fully met seven of the eight objectives set in Chapter 1 and partly met the eighth, with two substitutions (Snowflake Tasks instead of Airflow, and CSV export instead of a live Power BI connection) and one honest boundary: it runs on simulated data.

8.1 Against the objectives

Objective Met? Evidence
1. Realistic, imperfect data with a known truth Yes Seeded simulator; corruption manifest
2. Lossless, duplicate-free ingestion with proof Yes Idempotent COPY INTO; delivery-log reconciliation
3. A clean model that answers operational questions Yes 9 dimensions, 8 facts; 10 analytics queries
4. Every layer tested against exact values Yes 40 + 25 V1 checks; 117 dbt tests; all passing
5. dbt rebuild proven identical Yes 18 + 13 tables MATCH by row count and hash
6. Production capabilities Yes, with one substitution Incremental model, SCD2, task graph with quality gate, Stream alerts, RBAC, masking, volume monitoring; Tasks instead of Airflow
7. Forecast and dashboard Partly Forecast demonstrates the method on one week of data; dashboard reads CSV exports, not a live connection
8. Professional documentation Yes Incident report, README, commented code, this report

8.2 Answers to the research questions

RQ1 — Can messy feeds be integrated into one trustworthy model, and can that trust be proven? Yes. Trust here is not a claim but a set of passing checks with different jobs. Reconciliation proves nothing was lost in ingestion. Ground-truth tests prove the numbers are right. The parallel run proves the dbt rebuild changed nothing. Any one of them alone would leave a gap; together they cover ingestion, transformation and change.

RQ2 — Which failures pass silently through standard checks? Two kinds: a source that is honest but incomplete (Incident C), and a field whose label is wrong (the time-zone trap). Neither breaks a schema, a count or a key. Both needed checks based on expected behaviour — what normal volume looks like, and what a real UTC value looks like — rather than on rules about individual rows.

RQ3 — Can one disruption be traced to its impact? Yes, through aircraft rotations, passenger connections and bags, as the EK103 and FLT-0010 chains show. The enabling decisions were a shared flight identity derived from source fields, consistent surrogate keys, and recursive SQL to follow rotations.

RQ4 — What moves scripts to a production-style pipeline? The SQL logic changed surprisingly little between V1 and V2. What changed was everything around it: idempotent loads, incremental processing, a quality gate that stops bad loads, an audit log, version control, declared grants and masking that survive rebuilds, and documented incidents. Production readiness is mostly about what happens when things go wrong.

8.3 Limitations

  • Simulated data. Real feeds bring problems I did not model, such as encoding errors, corrupt or truncated files and partial uploads. The results show the platform handles realistic imperfections, not every imperfection.
  • Scale. One week, 20 aircraft and about half a million bag scans. Volume is a generator setting, but I have not tested the platform at airline scale, where warehouse sizing, clustering and partition pruning would matter.
  • Full rebuilds. Apart from int_bag_scans, models are rebuilt in full on every run. That is simple and naturally handles late data at this size, but would be costly at scale.
  • Orchestration scope. Tasks orchestrate work inside Snowflake but nothing outside it. Airflow was planned and not delivered because of a local installation blocker.
  • Simulated streaming. Live events are inserted with SQL to imitate a feed. A production design would use Snowpipe Streaming or Kafka.
  • Access testing. Role switching inside one user cannot fully prove least privilege, because secondary roles stay active; a separate test user is needed.
  • Forecasting. One week of history is too short for weekly or seasonal patterns, so the forecast demonstrates the method only.
  • Dashboard freshness. Power BI reads CSV exports, so the dashboard is a point-in-time view rather than a live control tower.
  • Shared stage. Truth files and corrupted feeds share one stage; production would separate them strictly.
  • No CI/CD yet. Tests run on every build, but not automatically on every code change.

8.4 What I would change if this became a real system

  1. Put the dbt project under CI: every pull request runs dbt build against a development schema, and nothing merges unless every test passes.
  2. Separate development and production environments, with production deployed only from the main branch.
  3. Replace simulated events with Snowpipe Streaming or Kafka, and make alerts notify people (for example, by email or a messaging channel), not just insert rows.
  4. Move the stable, high-volume models to incremental, and size and cluster the warehouse based on measured query patterns.
  5. Manage warehouses, roles, grants and policies with Terraform, so the platform can be rebuilt from code.
  6. Add freshness checks and alerting on every source, so a feed that stops arriving is noticed within the hour.
  7. Connect Power BI live to Snowflake, with row-level security mirroring Snowflake roles.

Chapter 9

9. How I learned — the skills behind the project

This project was as much a learning plan as a build. I set myself a rule at the start: never use a tool before understanding the problem it solves. For every major topic, I worked through the same sequence — what it is, why it exists, how it works internally, where it sits in a real data platform, what the alternatives are, what it does not solve — then a small standalone example, then the real implementation, and finally the production questions: what happens if it fails, if data is duplicated, if it arrives late, if the schema changes, if the volume grows?

Skill What I learned Where it lives in AERORESILIENCE Evidence

9.2 Lessons I will carry forward

A pipeline that runs is not a pipeline that is right. Every one of my early versions "worked" — no errors, plausible numbers — and several were wrong. Only exact-value tests showed it.

Trust the format, not the label. The time-zone trap taught me to verify what data is, not what it says it is.

The quiet failures are the dangerous ones. A crashed job gets noticed. A feed that sends 2% of its data with a perfectly valid file does not.

Design for re-running. Idempotent loads, deterministic de-duplication and merge-based incremental models mean that the answer to almost any failure is "fix it and run it again".

Write down what went wrong. The incident report and the masking story are, I think, the most convincing parts of this project, because they show how I think when something breaks.

Adapt without stalling. When Airflow would not install, I did not stop. I implemented the same concepts with the tools I had and recorded the gap honestly.

Chapter 10

10. Conclusion and future work

10.1 Conclusion

AERORESILIENCE shows that airline disruption chains can be made visible by integrating data that normally lives in separate systems — and that the integration can be proven correct, not just assumed. Starting from deliberately messy feeds, the platform delivers a tested star schema in which a single fault can be followed from a missing part, to a grounded aircraft, to late flights, misconnected passengers and mishandled bags.

The most valuable lessons were not about any one tool. A pipeline that runs is not the same as a pipeline that is right. The failures that matter most are the silent ones. And the engineering around the SQL — idempotency, reconciliation, quality gates, audit logs, access control and honest documentation — is what makes data trustworthy enough to act on.

The project also answered a personal question. I wanted to know whether I could build, without office experience, the kind of platform a professional data team would build. Every layer, test and incident in this report is my evidence that I can — and all of it is open for inspection in the repository.

It began with a friend stuck at an airport. It ends with a platform that would have shown, hour by hour, why he was stuck and who else was stuck with him. That is the kind of work I want to do.

10.2 Future work

Priority Improvement Why

2 Apache Airflow orchestration that replays the delivery log Orchestrate beyond Snowflake with industry-standard tooling
3 Kafka or Snowpipe Streaming for live events Replace simulated inserts with a true stream
4 Terraform for warehouses, roles and policies Rebuild the whole platform reproducibly from code

Operational notes

  • After any change to dbt files, redeploy the dbt project, or the task graph will keep running the old version.
  • After testing governance, always finish with USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN; and USE SECONDARY ROLES ALL; — dbt needs secondary roles on.
  • To save trial credits, suspend T1_LOAD_BRONZE and T_BAG_ALERTS when not demonstrating them. SHOW TASKS IN ACCOUNT; should show every task as suspended.
  • Re-creating only T1 breaks its link to T2. Always re-create all three tasks together, in order.

A singular test in dbt is a SELECT that returns the rows that break the rule. The test passes when the query returns nothing. For example, the "no teleport" test returns any flight whose origin differs from the destination of the same aircraft's previous flight.
