Appendix D

Appendix D — Glossary

Term Meaning
Accumulating snapshot A fact table with one row per process instance, updated as the process reaches milestones (for example, a bag's journey)
AOG (aircraft on ground) An aircraft that cannot fly until a fault is fixed, often while waiting for a part
BRONZE / SILVER / GOLD The medallion layers: raw as received, cleaned, and business-ready
Business key The identifier the business uses for something, such as an aircraft registration
CDC (change data capture) Tracking which rows are new or changed since the last read
Data contract An agreement about the shape and meaning of data a source will send
dbt A tool that builds, tests and documents SQL transformations as version-controlled code
DAG Directed acyclic graph: steps and their dependencies, with no loops
Degenerate dimension An identifier kept on a fact table without its own dimension table
Delivery log A control file recording when each source file arrived and how many records it declared
Grain Exactly what one row of a table represents
HASH_AGG A Snowflake function producing one fingerprint for a whole set of rows
Idempotent Safe to run more than once: the second run changes nothing
Incremental model A dbt model that processes only new data on each run and merges it in
Lineage The record of where data came from and what transformed it
Load metadata Snowflake's record of which files a table has already loaded
Masking policy A rule that returns real or masked column values depending on the user's role
MEL (Minimum Equipment List) The rules for which faults allow an aircraft to keep flying: NO-GO, GO-IF or GO
Medallion architecture Organising data into BRONZE, SILVER and GOLD layers of increasing quality
MERGE A SQL statement that inserts new rows and updates existing ones in one operation
Minimum connection time The shortest connection an airport considers achievable for passengers and bags
Observability Monitoring data over time (volume, freshness, schema) to spot unusual behaviour
Orchestration Running pipeline steps in order, on schedule, with retries and logging
Parallel run Running old and new pipelines side by side and proving their outputs match
Periodic snapshot A fact table with one row per entity per time period, such as stock per hour
Quality gate A check that stops downstream steps from running if it fails
RBAC Role-based access control: permissions are granted to roles, roles to users
Reactionary delay Delay caused by an earlier delay, usually an aircraft arriving late from its previous flight
Reconciliation Comparing what was received with what was declared or expected
Rotation The sequence of flights one aircraft flies
SCD Type 2 Slowly changing dimension that keeps history by closing old rows and adding new ones
Schema drift A source changing its structure (columns renamed, added or removed)
Schema-on-read Storing data without enforcing types, and applying structure when it is read
Secondary roles Snowflake roles that stay active in the background alongside the primary role
Snapshot (dbt) dbt's built-in implementation of SCD Type 2
Stage A Snowflake location where files are stored before loading
Star schema Facts in the centre, joined to the dimensions that describe them
Stream A Snowflake object that tracks changes to a table since it was last consumed
Surrogate key A system-generated key used to join facts to dimensions
Task A Snowflake object that runs SQL on a schedule or after another task
Transaction fact A fact table with one row per business event
VARIANT Snowflake's column type for semi-structured data such as JSON
Watermark The point up to which data has been processed, used by incremental loads

Appendix E

Appendix E — Questions I expect, and my answers

Why did you use a medallion architecture? Because it separates three different questions: what did the source send, what is true, and what does the business need. Keeping BRONZE untouched meant that when I found the time-zone bug, I fixed one SILVER rule and rebuilt — I never had to ask the source to resend anything.

Why Snowflake and not PostgreSQL? PostgreSQL could hold this data volume, but Snowflake gave me separated storage and compute, native JSON, and Streams, Tasks, masking policies and ML in one platform. The trade-off is lock-in: those features are Snowflake-specific.

Why dbt, if your SQL already worked? Working SQL scripts have no dependency management, no declared tests and no lineage. dbt turned them into a codebase I can test, version and deploy. I proved the migration changed nothing with a parallel run: row counts and HASH_AGG fingerprints on 31 tables, all matching.

How did you handle duplicates? At two levels. Exact duplicates are removed with QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() ... = 1, ordered deterministically so the same copy always wins. Messages re-sent with new IDs are removed by semantic de-duplication on their content. In the incremental model, MERGE on scan_id means a re-sent scan updates its row instead of adding one.

How did you handle late data? Full rebuilds naturally include it. In the incremental model, the watermark is arrival time, not event time. A late file has old event times but a new arrival time, so filtering on event time would skip it silently. Late rows are also flagged with received_late.

How did you handle schema changes? Incident B. I detected it by inspecting file headers, fixed it with name-based loading and schema evolution, and added a daily drift check using LAG() to compare each file's header with the previous one. In dbt, on_schema_change = 'fail' stops the incremental model rather than letting it drift silently.

How did you make the pipeline idempotent? COPY INTO skips files it has already loaded, de-duplication is deterministic, models are rebuilt or merged on a unique key, and setup scripts use IF NOT EXISTS. The answer to almost any failure is "fix it and run it again".

What happens if a load is incomplete? T2 compares rows loaded with the delivery log. Any mismatch is logged and raises an error, the task fails, and T3 — the dbt build — never runs. Bad data is stopped, not published.

What is the difference between testing and observability in your project? Tests check rules about rows. Incident C passed every rule: the Frankfurt file was valid and complete according to its own header. Only a volume check against Frankfurt's normal level caught that 98% of its scans were missing.

How did you secure personal data? An analyst role that can read only the marts, and a masking policy on passenger name and email. Both are re-applied by dbt on every build. I also found and fixed a real issue: secondary roles made my first policy appear to work for the wrong reason.

How would you scale it? Make more models incremental, cluster large tables on their most-filtered columns, size warehouses from measured workloads, separate load and transform warehouses, and replace simulated events with Snowpipe Streaming or Kafka.

How would you deploy it properly? Git for all code, CI that runs dbt build on every pull request against a development schema, production deployed only from the main branch, and infrastructure defined in Terraform.

What would you do differently? Set up CI and a separate development environment from day one, write the data contracts for each feed before building the loads, and build observability (freshness and volume) alongside BRONZE rather than as a later version.
